g11-physics-up6-t1.overview: Two charges push or pull with a force that follows an inverse-square law — the same geometry as gravity, but vastly stronger and able to attract OR repel. Coulomb's law is the foundation stone of electrostatics.
objectives: State Coulomb's law and apply F = kQ₁Q₂/r²
Use the constant k = 9×10⁹ N·m²/C² (and ε₀)
Determine force direction from charge signs (like repel, unlike attract)
Superpose forces from multiple charges (vector sum)
Compare electric and gravitational forces quantitatively
g11-physics-up6-t1.simple: Charge pushes on charge. The strength: multiply the two charges, divide by the square of their distance, times a big constant (9 billion). Double a charge → double the force. Double the distance → force drops to a QUARTER. Same signs shove apart; opposite signs yank together. Several charges? Compute each force separately, then add them as vectors — nature doesn't know you're doing bookkeeping.
g11-physics-up6-t1.detailed:
The law: F = k·|Q₁Q₂|/r², with k = 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m². Force acts along the line joining the centres; magnitude uses |charges|, direction from signs: like → repulsion, unlike → attraction. Newton's third law holds: each charge feels the SAME magnitude force.

Inverse-square intuition: the influence spreads over spheres of area 4πr² — double distance, same 'amount of push' covers 4× the area → quarter intensity. Same geometry as gravity and light.

Superposition: net force on a charge = VECTOR sum of the pairwise forces from every other charge. Compute magnitudes with Coulomb, draw directions, add by components (Grade 11 Unit 2 skills return!). Symmetric arrangements often cancel — look for it before calculating.

Electric vs gravitational: both inverse-square, both ∝ product of 'charge' (mass vs Q). But k is astronomically bigger than G (6.67×10⁻¹¹): two protons repel electrically ~10³⁶ times harder than they attract gravitationally. Gravity wins only in neutral bulk matter (planets) because mass is always positive and adds up, while +/− charges cancel.

Medium effect: in a material, force weakens: F = kQ₁Q₂/(εᵣr²) with εᵣ > 1 (relative permittivity; vacuum εᵣ = 1). Problems assume air/vacuum unless stated.

Equilibrium of charges: a third charge placed where two forces cancel feels zero net force — solve by setting magnitudes equal with distances as unknowns (watch: the null point lies BETWEEN unlike charges, outside the smaller one for like charges).

keyTerms.def: SI unit of charge; e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C per proton/electron.
N·m²/C² — Coulomb's constant, 1/(4πε₀).
F ∝ 1/r² — double distance, quarter force.
Net force = vector sum of individual pairwise forces.
Charge comes in whole multiples of e: Q = ne.
Position where net electric force on a test charge is zero.

formulas.meaning: Force between two point charges.

workedExamples.problem: Two small spheres carry +4 µC and −6 µC and are 20 cm apart. Find the force between them and state its nature.
workedExamples.answer: 5.4 N of ATTRACTION (unlike signs) — each sphere feels 5.4 N (third law).

workedExamples.problem: By what factor does the force change if both charges double AND the distance doubles?
workedExamples.answer: No change — the charge doubling (×4) exactly cancels the distance doubling (÷4). Classic proportionality trap.

workedExamples.problem: Charges +Q at x = 0 and +4Q at x = 30 cm. Find the point where a test charge feels zero net force.
workedExamples.given: Like charges → null point between them.
workedExamples.formula: Set field/force magnitudes equal: kQ/x² = k4Q/(0.3−x)².
workedExamples.answer: 10 cm from +Q (20 cm from +4Q) — closer to the smaller charge, as expected; distances ratio 1:2 = √(1:4) = √charge ratio.

workedExamples.problem: Three charges sit on a line: A = +2 µC at 0, B = −3 µC at 10 cm, C = +5 µC at 25 cm. Find the net force on B.
workedExamples.substitution: A pulls B right (attraction): F = 9e9×6e-12/0.01² = 540 N (+x). C pulls B right? No — B(−) and C(+): attraction pulls B toward C = +x: F = 9e9×15e-12/0.15² = 6 N (+x).
workedExamples.answer: ≈546 N toward C — note how the NEARBY charge dominates (inverse square: 540 vs 6 N).

workedExamples.problem: Compare the electric and gravitational force between two protons 1 nm apart. (m_p = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹)
workedExamples.formula: F_e = ke²/r²; F_g = Gm²/r² — ratio is r-independent.
workedExamples.answer: Electric repulsion is ~10³⁶ times gravity — gravity is irrelevant in particle physics; it only rules planets because matter is electrically neutral.

commonMistakes: Plugging charges WITH signs into F = kQ₁Q₂/r² and getting a 'negative force' — use magnitudes, then set direction from 'like repel, unlike attract'.
Forgetting to square r (and to convert cm → m BEFORE squaring).
Microcoulombs: 1 µC = 10⁻⁶ C — dropping the exponent is the #1 numerical error.
Adding force magnitudes instead of vectors in superposition.
Thinking the bigger charge feels a bigger force — third law: equal magnitudes.
Doubling r and expecting half the force — it's inverse-SQUARE (¼).
Null point for LIKE charges placed outside the pair (it's between them, nearer the smaller).
applications: Atomic structure: electron–nucleus Coulomb attraction holds atoms (why atoms are ~10⁻¹⁰ m).
Chemical bonding & reactions are Coulomb interactions at heart.
Photocopiers/laser printers: charged toner follows Coulomb paths to paper.
Electrostatic precipitators: charged pollution particles pulled from factory smoke.
Spray painting: charged paint wraps to grounded objects evenly.
Lightning: charge separation in clouds builds Coulomb forces until air breaks down.
g11-physics-up6-t1.summary: F = kQ₁Q₂/r² (k = 9×10⁹): along the join, like repel/unlike attract, equal-and-opposite pairs. Inverse-square: 2r → ¼F. Superpose pairwise forces as vectors — nearby charges dominate. Q = ne (quantised). Electric force crushes gravity by 10³⁶; it builds atoms, chemistry and lightning.

g11-physics-up6-t2.overview: Charge doesn't reach across empty space — it edits the space around it. The electric field is that edit: force per unit charge at every point. Field-line pictures make the invisible architecture of electricity visible and predictable.
objectives: Define E = F/Q and state its direction convention
Compute field of a point charge E = kQ/r² and superpose fields
Draw and interpret field-line patterns (point, pair, plates)
Analyse uniform fields between parallel plates: E = V/d
Predict motion of charges placed in fields (including projectile paths)
g11-physics-up6-t2.simple: An electric field is a 'push map': at every point, how much force would a positive test charge feel there? E = F/Q, measured in N/C (or V/m — same thing). A positive charge's field arrows point OUT (it repels tests); negative points IN. Field lines never cross, bunch where the field is strong, and run perpendicular to surfaces. Between two flat charged plates the field is uniform — same everywhere — so a charge gets yanked with constant force, tracing a parabola like a thrown ball.
g11-physics-up6-t2.detailed:
Definition: E = F/q₀ (force per unit POSITIVE test charge), N/C = V/m. Vector field filling space; source charges create it, other charges experience it. Force on any charge: F = qE — along E if q > 0, opposite if q < 0 (electrons fight the arrows).

Point charge field: E = kQ/r², radial: outward for +, inward for −. Superposition: E_net = vector sum of each source's E at the point (add components). Dipole (±q separated): field lines leave +, curve to −; mid-plane field points from + toward −.

Field-line rules (drawing discipline): start on +, end on − (or infinity); tangent = field direction; density = strength; NEVER cross (field has one direction per point); meet conductors at right angles; closer spacing near sharp points (why lightning rods are pointy).

Uniform field (parallel plates): E = V/d everywhere between them (edge fringing ignored). A charge released feels constant F = qE → constant acceleration a = qE/m → straight-line motion along the field, or PARABOLIC motion if it enters sideways (exactly like projectile motion with g replaced by qE/m — cathode-ray tubes and oscilloscopes steer electron beams this way).

Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium: E = 0 INSIDE the material (otherwise charges would keep moving); excess charge sits on the SURFACE; field at the surface ⊥ to it. Charge injected inside a hollow conductor migrates fully outside (Faraday cage — cars and lifts protect you from lightning).

Field vs force distinction: E exists whether or not a test charge is there; F = qE happens only when a charge occupies the field. The map vs the journey.

keyTerms.def: Force per unit positive charge; N/C or V/m.
Tiny + charge that probes a field without disturbing it.
Arrows showing direction; density shows strength.

workedExamples.problem: A charge of 4 µC feels a force of 0.02 N in a field. Find E. What force would 10 µC feel at the same spot?
workedExamples.answer: E = 5000 N/C (the spot's property — unchanged); the bigger charge simply samples it harder.

workedExamples.problem: Find the electric field 30 cm from a +9 nC point charge, and the force on an electron placed there.
workedExamples.substitution: E = 9e9 × 9e-9 / 0.09 = 900 N/C, directed AWAY from +Q. F = 1.6e-19 × 900.
workedExamples.calculation: F = 1.44×10⁻¹⁶ N toward Q (electron is negative → force opposite E).
workedExamples.answer: 900 N/C outward; electron pulled in with 1.4×10⁻¹⁶ N — tiny force, but on tiny mass: a = F/mₑ ≈ 1.6×10¹⁴ m/s²!

workedExamples.problem: Two plates 5 cm apart have 200 V across them. Find E. An electron enters horizontally at 2×10⁷ m/s through a 10 cm long field region — estimate its vertical deflection.
workedExamples.formula: E = V/d; a = eE/mₑ; t = L/vₓ; y = ½at².
workedExamples.answer: ≈8.8 mm deflection — parabolic steering, exactly how oscilloscope tubes paint the screen.

workedExamples.problem: Two charges +Q (left) and +Q (right) are 20 cm apart. Describe the field at the midpoint and at a point on the line 5 cm from the left charge.
workedExamples.substitution: Midpoint: equal magnitudes kQ/0.1², opposite directions → cancel. At 5 cm: E_left = kQ/0.05² (rightward), E_right = kQ/0.15² (leftward).
workedExamples.answer: Midpoint E = 0 (symmetry cancellation); off-centre the nearer charge dominates — field pushes away from the close +Q.

commonMistakes: Pointing field lines INTO a positive charge (they leave +, enter −).
Forgetting electrons feel force OPPOSITE the field arrows.
Crossing field lines in drawings — impossible; one direction per point.
Adding field magnitudes without direction (fields are vectors — components!).
Thinking E inside a conductor is 'small' — in equilibrium it is exactly ZERO.
Using E = kQ/r² for parallel plates (that's point charges; plates use E = V/d).
Confusing N/C with force — E is the map; F = qE is the journey.
applications: Oscilloscopes & old TVs: plate fields deflect electron beams pixel by pixel.
Inkjet printers: charged droplets steered by fields to place dots.
Lightning rods: sharp points concentrate field (E huge near tips) to trigger a controlled discharge.
Air filters & precipitators: fields drag charged soot from smoke.
Faraday cages: microwave ovens keep radiation in; cars keep lightning out.
Touchscreens (capacitive): your finger distorts the surface field grid.
g11-physics-up6-t2.summary: E = F/q₀ (N/C = V/m): force-per-charge map; point charges give E = kQ/r² radially; superpose as vectors. Lines leave +, enter −, never cross, density = strength. Parallel plates: uniform E = V/d → charges accelerate constantly → parabolas (CRTs). Conductors: E = 0 inside, ⊥ at surface — Faraday cages.

Test charge q enters the field
It feels F = qE (+ along, − opposite)

g11-physics-up6-t3.overview: Fields tell you the force; potential tells you the energy. Voltage is potential ENERGY per charge — the accountant's view of electrostatics — and the work–energy link V = W/Q makes circuits, sparks and electron beams calculable without vector headaches.
objectives: Define electric potential V = W/Q and potential difference
Relate work, charge and voltage: W = QV
Compute potentials of point charges V = kQ/r (scalar!) and superpose
Connect field and potential: E = V/d (uniform) and equipotential geometry
Use energy conservation: ½mv² = qV for accelerated charges
g11-physics-up6-t3.simple: Voltage = energy per coulomb. A 12 V battery gives every coulomb that passes through it 12 joules. Moving charge between two points costs or releases W = QV. Potential from a point charge is just kQ/r — a plain NUMBER (no arrows — it's scalar, so adding potentials is simple arithmetic, easier than adding fields!). Equipotential lines join equal-voltage points and always sit perpendicular to field lines. Fall through 100 V and a proton picks up 100 eV of kinetic energy — the unit particle physicists live by.
g11-physics-up6-t3.detailed:
Potential V: work done bringing a unit POSITIVE charge from infinity to the point (J/C = volt). Scalar. Point charge: V = kQ/r (signed: + around positives, − around negatives). Superposition: V_total = ΣkQᵢ/rᵢ — algebraic sum, no components. (Compare E: vector sum — potentials are the easy route.)

Potential difference: ΔV = V_B − V_A = W/Q (work per charge moving A→B). Voltage is always BETWEEN two points; 'the potential at a point' is relative to infinity/earth chosen as zero.

Work and energy: W = QΔV. Positive charge 'falls' from high V to low V, gaining KE (like a ball falling in height). Negative charges climb toward high V. Energy conservation: qΔV + ½mv² = constant → an electron accelerated through 100 V gains KE = e×100 = 100 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁷ J → v = √(2×1.6e-17/9.1e-31) ≈ 5.9×10⁶ m/s.

Field–potential link: E = −ΔV/Δd (field points downhill in potential, toward decreasing V). Uniform plates: E = V/d. Equipotentials: surfaces of equal V; perpendicular to field lines; NO work moving along one (force ⊥ motion). Closer equipotential spacing = stronger field.

Conductors: entire conductor is one equipotential (E = 0 inside → no V change along it); charge distributes to make its surface smooth-voltage; sharp points crowd both field AND potential gradient (corona, lightning rods).

Sign discipline: V can be negative (near −Q); work by the FIELD = −ΔU = −qΔV. A charge released from rest moves to REDUCE its potential energy U = qV (positives downhill in V, negatives uphill).

keyTerms.def: 1 J/C — energy per unit charge.

workedExamples.problem: Parallel plates 4 cm apart have 600 V. Find E. A charge of +5 µC moves from the + plate to the − plate. Find the work done BY the field and describe its motion.

workedExamples.calculation: W = 3 mJ (field does positive work; KE grows by 3 mJ).
workedExamples.answer: E = 15 kV/m; the + charge accelerates uniformly toward the − plate, gaining 3 mJ — constant force, parabolic if it enters sideways.

commonMistakes: Treating potential as a vector — it's a signed SCALAR; just add numbers.
Dropping charge signs in V = kQ/r (−Q gives −V).
Confusing E (N/C, force view) with V (J/C, energy view) — both describe the same field differently.
Saying work is done moving a charge ALONG an equipotential — zero work (force ⊥ path).
Forgetting electrons move toward HIGHER potential (they lose U = qV with q negative).
Using W = QV with ΔV in the wrong direction — track 'from A to B'.
Mixing eV and J: 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J, not 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ eV = 1 J.
applications: CRTs & electron microscopes: kV potentials set beam speed and resolution.
Particle accelerators: every stage adds energy in eV (MeV, GeV beams).
Power transmission: high voltage = less current for the same power = less I²R loss.
Lightning: cloud–ground potential differences of 10⁸ V break down the air.
Touch ID / capacitive sensors: tiny potential changes detect fingerprints.
Neuroscience: nerve signals are membrane potential differences (~70 mV).

W = QΔV; charges fall to lower U = qV (positives downhill in V, electrons uphill). E = V/d links the slope; equipotentials ⊥ field lines, zero work along them. eV: the particle-physics energy coin.

g11-physics-up6-t4.overview: Current is charge flowing, resistance is the traffic jam, and voltage is the pressure driving them. Ohm's law V = IR ties the three together — and the non-ohmic characters (lamps, diodes, thermistors) reveal how materials really behave.
objectives: Define current I = Q/t and resistance R = V/I
Apply Ohm's law and read/plot V–I characteristics
Use the microscopic resistance model R = ρL/A
Explain non-ohmic behaviour: filament lamp, diode, thermistor curves
Calculate power dissipation P = VI = I²R = V²/R
g11-physics-up6-t4.simple: Current = coulombs per second through a wire (amps). Voltage = the push per coulomb. Resistance = how much the material fights the flow (ohms). Ohm's law: V = IR — for a METAL at steady temperature, doubling the push doubles the flow. But not everything obeys: a bulb's filament resists MORE as it heats (curve bends), a diode only allows flow one way (valve), a thermistor's resistance drops when hot (sensor). Power: P = VI — how fast electrical energy becomes heat/light.
g11-physics-up6-t4.detailed:
Current: I = Q/t (ampere = C/s). Conventional current = + charge flow direction (opposite to electron drift). Drift is slow (~mm/s) but the field propagates near light-speed — that's why the lamp lights instantly. Series: same I everywhere; junction: ΣI in = ΣI out (charge conservation — Kirchhoff's current law).

Resistance & Ohm's law: R = V/I (Ω = V/A). Ohm's law is an EXPERIMENTAL statement for a fixed temperature: V ∝ I. Microscopic origin: electrons scatter off lattice vibrations; more heat → more scattering → higher R in metals. Geometry: R = ρL/A — longer wire more resistance, thicker less; ρ = resistivity (material): copper 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, nichrome 1.1×10⁻⁶ (heaters!), glass ~10¹⁰+.

V–I graphs (the exam's favourite):
• Ohmic resistor: straight line through origin; gradient = 1/R (or R = V/I at any point).
• Filament lamp: S-curve flattening at high V — heating raises R, so current grows slower; R increases with temperature.
• Diode: ~zero current until ≈0.6–0.7 V (Si) forward, then shoots up; blocks reverse entirely — a one-way valve (rectifiers).
• Thermistor (NTC): R falls steeply when heated — sensitive temperature sensors/alarms.
• Fixed resistor: linear both directions.

Power & energy: P = VI (watts); with Ohm's law: P = I²R = V²/R. Energy E = Pt. Fuses: I²R heating melts the wire above rating. 'Kilowatt-hour' = energy of 1 kW for 1 h = 3.6 MJ — the billing unit.

EMF vs pd: EMF (ε) = energy per charge the source SUPPLIES (volts, measured open-circuit); pd (V) = energy per charge USED across a component. Real batteries have internal resistance r: V_terminal = ε − Ir — why headlights dim when starting an engine.

workedExamples.problem: A heater draws 5 A from a 240 V mains. Find its resistance, power, and the energy in 2 hours (kWh and J).
workedExamples.formula: R = V/I; P = VI; E = Pt.
workedExamples.answer: 48 Ω, 1.2 kW, 2.4 kWh — at ~$0.1/kWh that's 24 cents of heat.

workedExamples.problem: Find the resistance of 50 m of copper wire of cross-section 2 mm² (ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m). What voltage drop does 10 A suffer along it?
workedExamples.calculation: R = 0.425 Ω; V = 10 × 0.425 = 4.25 V (loss = I²R = 42.5 W wasted as heat).
workedExamples.answer: 0.43 Ω — small but real: this is why power grids run at HIGH voltage (tiny I → I²R losses collapse).

workedExamples.problem: A filament lamp's V–I curve passes through (2 V, 0.5 A) and (12 V, 1.0 A). Compute R at each point and explain the change.
workedExamples.calculation: Resistance tripled as the filament heated from dim to bright.
workedExamples.answer: 4 Ω cold-ish → 12 Ω hot: lattice vibrations increase with temperature, scattering electrons — the lamp is NON-ohmic; Ohm's law fails here.

workedExamples.problem: A battery has EMF 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω. It drives 2.5 Ω. Find the circuit current and the terminal voltage.
workedExamples.calculation: V = 5 V (1 V 'lost' inside the battery, heating it).
workedExamples.answer: 2 A, terminal 5 V — under load a battery's output sags; the bigger the current, the bigger the sag.

workedExamples.problem: An NTC thermistor reads 10 kΩ at 20 °C and 2 kΩ at 60 °C. In a potential divider with a fixed 5 kΩ above it across 9 V, find the output (across the thermistor) at each temperature and explain the alarm use.
workedExamples.calculation: Output falls from 6 V to 2.6 V as it warms.
workedExamples.answer: Voltage drops with temperature — trigger a comparator at ~4 V and you have a fire alarm / thermostat; thermistors turn temperature into voltage.

commonMistakes: Saying 'current is used up' by components — charge is conserved; ENERGY is transferred (current in = current out of a resistor).
Applying V = IR to lamps/diodes as if R were constant — it's the ratio at a point, not a property.
Gradient confusion on V–I graphs: with V on the y-axis, gradient = R; with I on y, gradient = 1/R.
Forgetting to convert mm² to m² in R = ρL/A (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²).
Mixing EMF and terminal voltage — V = ε − Ir, not ε, when current flows.
P = V²/R uses the voltage ACROSS that resistor only.
Thinking electrons race through the wire at light speed — drift is mm/s; the FIELD is fast.
applications: Mains wiring: copper's low ρ sets wire gauges; fuses exploit I²R melting.
Heating appliances: nichrome (high ρ) coils in kettles, toasters, irons.
Rectifiers: diodes convert AC → DC in every phone charger.
Temperature control: thermistors in thermostats, batteries' BMS, incubators.
Grid transmission: high-voltage lines slash I²R losses over distance.
Light dimmers & volume knobs: potentiometers (variable R).
g11-physics-up6-t4.summary: I = Q/t; R = V/I; Ohm: V = IR at constant T (linear V–I through origin). Geometry: R = ρL/A. Non-ohmic cast: lamp (R↑ with heat), diode (one-way, 0.7 V), thermistor (R↓ with heat). Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; energy in kWh. Real sources: V = ε − Ir.

g11-physics-up6-t5.overview: A capacitor is an energy bucket measured in farads: two conductors, an insulator between, and charge stored on tap. From camera flashes to touchscreens to the smoothing circuits in every charger, capacitance is where electrostatics meets circuits.
objectives: Define C = Q/V and the farad
Compute energy stored: E = ½QV = ½CV² = Q²/2C
Combine capacitors in series (1/C sum) and parallel (direct sum)
Describe charging/discharging curves and the time constant RC
Explain dielectrics and real-world capacitor applications
g11-physics-up6-t5.simple: Two plates facing each other, separated by an insulator: push charge onto one and the other attracts it across the gap — energy parked in the electric field between them. Capacitance C = Q/V: how many coulombs per volt you can park (farads; real ones are µF). Bigger plates, closer, with a dielectric between = more farads. Series: smaller than the smallest (gap got longer). Parallel: adds up (area got bigger). They charge and discharge exponentially with time constant τ = RC — the heartbeat of timers and flash units.
g11-physics-up6-t5.detailed:
Definition: C = Q/V (farad = C/V). For a parallel-plate capacitor: C = ε₀εᵣA/d — area up, gap down, dielectric in → more capacitance. The dielectric (εᵣ > 1) polarises, weakening the internal field, letting MORE charge sit at the same voltage (capacitance ×εᵣ), and raises the breakdown voltage.

Stored energy: building charge against rising voltage costs work: E = ½QV = ½CV² = Q²/(2C). The ½ appears because voltage ramps from 0 to V as charge accumulates (average V = ½V). Energy lives in the field between the plates (density ∝ E²).

Combinations (mirror resistors, opposite rules):
• Parallel: same V, charges add → C_eq = C₁ + C₂ + ... (more plate area).
• Series: same Q, voltages add → 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (more gap). Smallest dominates.

Charging/discharging (RC circuits): Q(t) = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)) charging; Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC) discharging. Time constant τ = RC: after 1τ → 63% (charge) or 37% (decay); after 5τ ≈ complete. Current spikes then decays; voltage across the capacitor is the SMOOTH one — hence 'smoothing' in power supplies.

Graph shapes: V–t charging: rising exponential flattening at ε; discharging: falling exponential. Gradient at any point ∝ remaining gap to final — the hallmark of exponential processes (also seen in half-lives, next unit!).

Real uses: camera flash (store slowly, dump in milliseconds — huge power from small energy), smoothing ripples in DC supplies, coupling/decoupling in audio, touchscreens (finger changes local C), defibrillators (controlled discharge through the heart), keyboard keys.

keyTerms.def: Charge per volt, Q/V; farad (F).
Insulator between plates; raises C by εᵣ.
RC — 63% of a charge/discharge step per τ.
Capacitor filling the gaps between AC pulses in a DC supply.
Field so strong the dielectric conducts — capacitor destroyed.

workedExamples.problem: A 2200 µF capacitor is charged from a 9 V supply. Find its charge, stored energy, and the average power if it discharges fully in 0.2 s.
workedExamples.formula: Q = CV; E = ½CV²; P = E/t.
workedExamples.answer: 19.8 mC, 89 mJ — modest energy, but dumped fast it out-powers its size (the flash-camera trick).

workedExamples.problem: Combine 3 µF, 6 µF: find C for (a) parallel, (b) series. Then put (b) across 12 V — what charge and voltage does each capacitor get?
workedExamples.formula: Parallel sum; series reciprocal; Q same in series.
workedExamples.substitution: (a) 9 µF. (b) 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 = ½ → 2 µF. Series: Q = 2e-6×12 = 24 µC each.
workedExamples.answer: 9 µF parallel; 2 µF series; in series the SMALLER capacitor takes the LARGER voltage (opposite of resistors' voltage split!).

workedExamples.problem: A camera flash uses a 150 µF capacitor charged to 300 V, discharged in 2 ms. Find stored energy and peak power. Why can't a battery replace it directly?
workedExamples.answer: 6.75 J delivered at 3.4 kW — batteries can't dump that power rate; capacitors store energy SLOWLY and release it FASTER than any battery.

workedExamples.problem: RC timer: R = 500 kΩ, C = 100 µF across 12 V. Find τ, the capacitor voltage after 50 s of charging, and how long to reach 11.4 V (95%).
workedExamples.answer: τ = 50 s, 7.6 V after one τ, ~150 s to be 'fully' charged — exponential timers set wiper delays and blinking LEDs.

commonMistakes: Combining capacitors with resistor rules — they're INVERTED: parallel adds, series reciprocates.
Forgetting the ½ in E = ½CV² (voltage ramps up while charging).
In series capacitors, assuming voltage splits equally — it splits INVERSELY to C (small C, big V).
Thinking a capacitor 'passes DC' — steady DC is blocked; only transients/AC get through.
Reading τ as 'full charge time' — 1τ = 63%; full ≈ 5τ.
µF → F conversion: 1 µF = 10⁻⁶ F (and nF = 10⁻⁹).
Touching 'disconnected' capacitors — they hold charge (defibrillator-level energy in old TVs).
applications: Camera flashes & defibrillators: slow charge, millisecond discharge = kilowatts on demand.
Power supplies: smoothing capacitors fill the ripple between rectified AC peaks.
Touchscreens: your conductive finger changes capacitance at each grid point.
Timing circuits: RC constants set blinkers, wipers, 555 timers.
Coupling capacitors: pass audio AC, block DC bias between amplifier stages.
Keyboards & RAM: each bit is a microscopic capacitor's charge.
Wireless & radio: capacitors tune circuits with inductors (LC resonance).
g11-physics-up6-t5.summary: C = Q/V (farads): charge parked per volt in a plate-to-plate field. E = ½CV² (the ½ from the ramp). Plates: C = ε₀εᵣA/d — dielectrics multiply C. Parallel adds; series reciprocates (small C takes big V). RC: τ = RC, 63% per τ, 5τ done — exponential timers and smoothing. Flash = slow store, fast dump.

g11-physics-up6-t6.overview: Series and parallel are the two building blocks of every circuit ever wired — from torches to house wiring. This lesson assembles Kirchhoff's laws, potential dividers and the safety trio (fuse, earth, breaker) into the practical electricity around you.
objectives: Analyse series and parallel resistor networks (R_eq, current, voltage splits)
Apply Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws
Design and calculate potential dividers (including sensor inputs)
Explain household wiring: live/neutral/earth, fuses, circuit breakers, RCDs
Troubleshoot real circuits with meter logic (ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel)
g11-physics-up6-t6.simple: Series: one road, same traffic (current) everywhere; voltage splits across components; resistances ADD. Parallel: many roads; each branch gets the FULL voltage; currents split; resistance DROPS below the smallest branch (more paths = easier flow). Two Kirchhoff rules run everything: around any loop the voltage shares sum to the source; into any junction, current in = current out. In your wall: live carries, neutral returns, earth is the escape route; a fuse melts on overload; an RCD trips if current leaks to you.
g11-physics-up6-t6.detailed:
Series: I same through all; V = V₁ + V₂ + ... (KVL); R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + ... Voltage divides in proportion to R (potential divider). One component fails open → whole chain dead (old fairy lights).

Parallel: V same across each branch; I = I₁ + I₂ + ... (KCL); 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... Current divides INVERSELY to R. Household wiring is parallel: every appliance gets full mains voltage and switches independently; adding appliances lowers total R → raises total current → fuse limits it.

Kirchhoff's laws: KVL: ΣEMF = ΣIR around any closed loop (energy per charge conserved). KCL: ΣI_in = ΣI_out at any junction (charge conserved). These + Ohm's law solve any DC network.

Potential dividers: two resistors across V_in tap V_out = V_in × R₂/(R₁+R₂). Swap in a sensor (LDR, thermistor) → voltage becomes a measurement. Loading: drawing current from the tap shifts the ratio (use high-resistance meters).

Internal resistance in circuits: V_terminal = ε − Ir; maximum power transfer when R_load = r (audio matching).

Meter rules: ammeter in SERIES (near-zero R — don't want to block flow); voltmeter in PARALLEL (huge R — don't want to steal current). An ammeter across the supply = a short circuit (bang).

Household safety stack: live (≈230 V), neutral (near 0 V, returns current), earth (unused until needed). Fuse in live: melts if I exceeds rating (I²R heat). Circuit breaker: electromagnetic trip on overload, resettable. RCD/GFCI: detects imbalance live-vs-neutral (current leaking through a person to earth) and trips in ~30 ms at ~30 mA. Double insulation removes the earth requirement. Why earth works: it gives fault current a low-R path so the fuse blows BEFORE the case stays live.

keyTerms.def: Single path; same I; voltages add; R sums.
Branches share V; currents add; 1/R sums.
KVL (loop voltages) + KCL (junction currents) = conservation.
Series resistors tapping a fraction of the input voltage.
Sacrificial wire melting on overcurrent.
Leakage detector tripping in milliseconds.
Safety path making faults blow the fuse fast.

workedExamples.problem: R₁ = 6 Ω in series with a parallel pair (R₂ = 4 Ω, R₃ = 12 Ω), across 24 V. Find total resistance, total current, and the branch currents.
workedExamples.answer: 9 Ω, 2.67 A total; the LOW-resistance branch hogs the current (2 A vs 0.67 A — inverse ratio 3:1).

workedExamples.problem: Design a divider from 9 V giving 3 V open-circuit, drawing ≤ 5 mA from the supply. Choose R₁ and R₂.
workedExamples.formula: V_out = V_in R₂/(R₁+R₂); total R = V/I.
workedExamples.calculation: Pick R₂ = 600 Ω, R₁ = 1200 Ω (total 1.8 kΩ, I = 5 mA).
workedExamples.answer: R₁ = 1.2 kΩ (top), R₂ = 600 Ω (bottom) — add a load and the tap sags; that's loading error.

workedExamples.problem: An LDR (dark 50 kΩ, light 500 Ω) sits as the TOP resistor of a divider with a fixed 10 kΩ bottom across 6 V. Find V_out in light and dark, and how this switches a street lamp.
workedExamples.calculation: Output HIGH by day, LOW at night.
workedExamples.answer: Feed V_out to a comparator: below ~2 V → lamp ON. Swap LDR and resistor to invert the logic.

workedExamples.problem: A 13 A fuse protects a 230 V ring main. List the appliances that can run together: kettle 3 kW, iron 2.4 kW, heater 2 kW. Explain why adding the heater trips the fuse.
workedExamples.formula: I = P/V; parallel branches sum currents.
workedExamples.substitution: Kettle: 3000/230 = 13.0 A — already at the limit! Iron: 10.4 A; heater: 8.7 A.
workedExamples.calculation: Kettle alone ≈ 13 A; kettle + anything > 13 A → fuse melts (I²R heats its wire past melting).
workedExamples.answer: Only ONE heavy appliance per 13 A socket/ring — the fuse rating is the current budget; parallel loads spend it jointly.

workedExamples.problem: A faulty toaster makes its metal case live. Trace what happens (a) without an earth wire, (b) with earth, (c) with an RCD — and why 30 mA trips save lives.
workedExamples.formula: Safety path analysis (V = IR, body ~1–10 kΩ contact).
workedExamples.substitution: (a) Case sits at 230 V; the next person touching it completes the path — 230/2000 ≈ 0.1 A through the body: fibrillation territory. (b) Earth gives a ~1 Ω path → hundreds of amps → fuse blows instantly. (c) RCD compares live vs neutral; the leak through a person (≥30 mA) unbalances it → trip in <40 ms.
workedExamples.calculation: 30 mA AC through the chest can fibrillate; RCD threshold sits below that.
workedExamples.answer: Earth + fuse handle equipment faults; the RCD handles the PERSON fault — layered defence.

commonMistakes: Assuming current is 'used up' after the first bulb in series — same I everywhere; ENERGY drops.
Parallel thinking: more resistors = more resistance. It's LESS (more paths).
Divider formula upside-down: V_out uses the resistor you're tapping ACROSS in the numerator.
Ammeter wired in parallel (shorts the component) or voltmeter in series (breaks the circuit).
Adding currents in series or voltages across parallel branches — swap the rules.
Forgetting internal resistance when the battery is old/high-current.
Believing 'low voltage is safe' — 12 V through the body is harmless, but mains at 230 V through 2 kΩ skin is 115 mA: lethal; and RCDs exist because even mA matter.
Replacing a fuse with a thicker wire 'so it stops blowing' — you removed the safety margin, not the fault.
applications: Every home: parallel sockets, ring mains, per-circuit fuses/breakers, RCD protection.
Sensor electronics: dividers with LDRs (street lights), thermistors (alarms), potentiometers (volume).
LED strings: series chains for voltage stacking; parallel banks for reliability.
Battery packs: series for voltage, parallel for capacity (laptops, EVs).
Automotive: 12 V parallel loads, blade fuses per circuit.
Current sensing: shunt resistors (tiny R, measurable V) in multimeters and EVs.
g11-physics-up6-t6.summary: Series: one path, same I, V divides, R adds. Parallel: shared V, I divides, R shrinks. Kirchhoff: loops conserve energy (KVL), junctions conserve charge (KCL). Dividers turn resistance ratios into voltages — sensors ride on them. Meters: A in series, V in parallel. Household safety: live/neutral/earth + fuse + breaker + RCD, each guarding a different failure.

steps: Series section: same I, voltage drops
